title: Elodie and the Visitor
premise: August Zhou takes a teaching post in the fog-bound town of Hollowmere, where students vanish one by one and no one will say their names aloud. When he inherits his late grandmother's house, he discovers every family photograph now contains an empty chair that wasn't there before — and each time a chair appears, someone in town disappears. August realizes the 'Visitor' is counting its way through his bloodline, and that his estranged family, scattered and resentful, are all still on the list. To save them, August must gather the relatives he abandoned fifteen years ago, learn the ritual his grandmother died trying to finish, and offer the Visitor something it has never been given: a willing host. In the end, August sits in the extra chair himself, trading his place in photographs for his family's lives — and becomes the presence the next generation must explain away.
about_author: Ivo Eastwick is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent a decade collecting the small superstitions of isolated coastal towns before turning them into fiction. They write horror about families that love each other badly and houses that remember everything.

chapters.title: The Long Road to Hollowmere
chapters.summary: August's POV. August arrives in Hollowmere on a bus with too few passengers, taking the teaching post nobody local wanted. The town feels rehearsed, like a stage set between performances. Emotional beat: cautious hope masking fifteen years of running from family and memory.

chapters.title: Roll Call
chapters.summary: August's POV. On the first day, August counts twenty-nine students; the register lists thirty-four. When asked, the class goes silent and a girl named Wren says only, 'We don't count them out loud.' Emotional beat: first crack in the town's polite facade.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: August's POV. August moves into the inherited house on Lantern Row, finding grandma Ruth's belongings untouched since her death — including a wall of family photographs spanning decades. Emotional beat: grief tangled with guilt over years of unanswered letters.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: August's POV. In a 1998 photo of a birthday dinner, there's an empty chair at the table that August remembers not existing. In every later photo, the chair is there, closer to the head. Emotional beat: rational explanations begin to fail.

chapters.title: Colleagues Who Don't Look Up
chapters.summary: August's POV. August probes the vice-principal, Mr. Aldous, about missing students; Aldous answers in careful non-answers and warns him to keep his own count private. Emotional beat: isolation deepening — even allies speak in code.

chapters.title: Wren's List
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, the register's missing fifth student, reveals she keeps a notebook of every vanished classmate going back sixty years — all descendants of families on Lantern Row. Emotional beat: grim solidarity between outsiders.

chapters.title: Phone Calls Nobody Answers
chapters.summary: August's POV. August tries calling his estranged sister Marisol; the call connects but only breathing and faint furniture sounds answer. That night, a new photograph shows the chair pulled out, as if recently sat in. Emotional beat: dread becoming personal.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren shows August the abandoned building locals call the Counting House, where vanished students' belongings sit in labeled boxes, dusted and maintained by unseen hands. Emotional beat: horror of care — something is tending to the lost.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. In another city, Marisol receives August's voicemail and almost deletes it. She's been dreaming of a dinner table with one more seat every night. Emotional beat: resentment warring with the pull of blood.

chapters.title: Ruth's Journal, Part One
chapters.summary: August's POV. August finds grandma Ruth's journal hidden under floorboards: entries describing 'the Visitor' as a family guest that arrives when a generation forgets to invite it properly. Emotional beat: the past was never finished with them.

chapters.title: Parent-Teacher Night
chapters.summary: August's POV. At conferences, parents flinch when August mentions attendance. One mother whispers that her son didn't leave — 'he was counted,' she says, then denies saying it. Emotional beat: the town's complicity revealed as fear, not malice.

chapters.title: Uncle Theo Arrives
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo Zhou, black-sheep uncle and Ruth's son, shows up uninvited, claiming he dreamed the house needed him. He hasn't spoken to August in fifteen years. Emotional beat: awkward, barbed reunion — found family beginning to assemble from actual family.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Want
chapters.summary: August's POV. August experiments: burning a photo does nothing; the image reappears in another frame. The chair in the newest picture now faces the camera. Emotional beat: helplessness — the rules are real and unreadable.

chapters.title: The Fifth Seat
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren admits she transferred to Hollowmere deliberately: her grandmother was counted in 1974, and she came to understand why. She and August compare notes and realize the Visitor works down bloodlines, one branch at a time. Emotional beat: two lonely people becoming a team.

chapters.title: Aldous's Confession
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. Vice-principal Aldous, drunk in his classroom, tells August he was the last teacher who tried to stop the count — his brother was taken in exchange for his silence. Emotional beat: broken mentorship; a warning written in scars.

chapters.title: Journal, Part Two: The Invitation
chapters.summary: August's POV. Ruth's journal describes a counter-ritual: the family must gather and formally invite the Visitor to dinner, offering it a chosen seat willingly filled — or it chooses for itself. Emotional beat: hope with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: Cousin Ida Refuses
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. August travels to bring cousin Ida home; she slams the door, blaming the Zhous for her mother's disappearance decades ago. Through the window, August sees an empty chair in her kitchen. Emotional beat: the cost of old wounds — denial doesn't exempt anyone.

chapters.title: Twenty-Nine Becomes Twenty-Six
chapters.summary: August's POV. Three students vanish in one week; the school holds no assemblies, sends no letters. Wren's notebook fills. August finds one student's desk left perfectly clean, a folded paper crane on top. Emotional beat: mourning without permission to grieve.

chapters.title: The Dinner Nobody Cooked
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo wakes at 3 a.m. to find the dining table set for six, food steaming, though he lives alone above the garage. He eats nothing but can't bring himself to clear it. Emotional beat: seduction of the uncanny — the Visitor is courteous.

chapters.title: Marisol Comes Home
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol arrives at Lantern Row with her teenage son Dev, refusing to explain the bruises on her arm or why she finally answered. The house's photos rearrange overnight: everyone gathered, smiling, one chair empty. Emotional beat: fragile reconciliation built on shared terror.

chapters.title: Dev Sees It First
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev, awake late, watches a tall figure in the hallway politely test the empty chair's sturdiness, then nod approvingly at him before dissolving into wallpaper shadow. No adult believes him — until they see the chair scratched. Emotional beat: the child as truth-teller.

chapters.title: Rules of Hospitality
chapters.summary: August's POV. Cross-referencing Ruth's journal with Wren's sixty-year records, August deduces the Visitor's law: it may only take those who have refused hospitality — the unreconciled, the door-slammers. Ida is next. Emotional beat: urgency fusing with moral clarity.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A storm seals the roads; the power fails town-wide except on Lantern Row, where every lamp burns steady. Wren realizes the house isn't being haunted — it's being prepared. Emotional beat: claustrophobic escalation.

chapters.title: Ida at the Door
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Ida arrives soaked and shaking, her kitchen chair found smashed and her locks turned by themselves. She apologizes to August in fragments. He lets her in, and the photographs settle, satisfied. Emotional beat: forgiveness as literal survival.

chapters.title: Aldous Doesn't Come to Work
chapters.summary: August's POV. Aldous vanishes; his classroom contains a new box in the Counting House style, labeled in his handwriting: FOR THE NEXT ONE. Inside is Ruth's missing final journal page. Emotional beat: mentor lost, torch passed.

chapters.title: The Final Page
chapters.summary: August's POV. Ruth's last page reveals her plan failed because she tried to trick the Visitor with a mannequin in the offered seat. It demands sincerity: a living volunteer who genuinely chooses to stay. Emotional beat: the trap's true shape — love cannot be faked.

chapters.title: Family Meeting
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. The whole household argues through the night: who could volunteer, whether running is possible, whether the Visitor would even accept August. Dev quietly studies the photographs. Emotional beat: found family forged in crisis, ugly and honest.

chapters.title: Dev's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev offers himself, reasoning the Visitor prefers the young; the chairs in the photos all turn toward his room overnight. August refuses absolutely, and the refusal costs him — every photo of August begins to fade. Emotional beat: sacrificial love colliding with parental terror.

chapters.title: What August Remembers
chapters.summary: August's POV. Fading, August recovers the suppressed memory: at nine, he broke Ruth's dinner invitation rule, told the knocking visitor nobody was home, and it took his father instead. The count began with his lie. Emotional beat: devastating self-recognition — he is the cause.

chapters.title: Confession at the Table
chapters.summary: Full household POV rotation. August confesses everything at the set table. Instead of recoiling, the family sets a seventh place — for him — and asks him to tell the whole story slowly, together. Emotional beat: grace; belonging earned through truth.

chapters.title: Preparing the Feast
chapters.summary: Theo and Marisol's POV. The family cooks Ruth's recipes from her journal, sets the table exactly as in the oldest photograph, and rehearses the invitation words. Wren stands guard with the notebook, reading names of the counted aloud so none are forgotten. Emotional beat: ritual as reclamation.

chapters.title: The Visitor Comes to Dinner
chapters.summary: August's POV. At midnight the door opens without knocking. The Visitor enters — familiar, wrong, wearing gestures borrowed from everyone August has lost. It pulls out the extra chair and waits. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into terrible hospitality.

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.summary: August's POV. August speaks the invitation honestly: acknowledging his lie, naming his dead, and offering himself willingly — not as sacrifice but as return. The Visitor studies him for a long, airless moment. Emotional beat: courage as acceptance rather than defiance.

chapters.title: The Choice It Offers
chapters.summary: Visitor's perspective, rendered obliquely. The Visitor reveals it is not a predator but a ledger-keeper, bound to collect what hospitality debts accrue; a sincere host may close the account. It shows August what sitting means: becoming the one who waits, who tends, who counts. Emotional beat: awe and grief entwined.

chapters.title: Sitting Down
chapters.summary: August's POV. August sits. The house exhales; the storm breaks; every vanished name in Wren's notebook gently crosses itself out as the counted are released back into memory, if not flesh. The photographs change: full tables, warm light, August's chair at the head. Emotional beat: transcendence through surrender.

chapters.title: Morning After the End
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The family wakes to ordinary sunlight. August is gone from every room but present in every photograph, smiling. The school register reads thirty-four again, all accounted for. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace — victory that feels like loss.

chapters.title: What We Tell the Children
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren closes her notebook and starts a new one: not a list of the lost, but a record of stories, so the next generation knows the rules and the reasons. Dev asks hard questions; the family answers honestly. Emotional beat: breaking cycles through remembrance.

chapters.title: Lantern Row, Years Later
chapters.summary: Dev's POV, grown. Dev now teaches at Hollowmere's school and lives in the house. Dinners are loud, chairs mismatched, doors always open to kin and stranger alike. Sometimes the extra chair sits at the table, and they set it anyway. Emotional beat: belonging as ongoing practice.

chapters.title: The New Teacher
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. A nervous new hire arrives in town, mentioning odd noises in an inherited house. Dev recognizes the look — fifteen years of explaining away — and invites them to Sunday dinner. Emotional beat: the found family extends its table; the cycle becomes care.

chapters.title: Elodie and the Visitor
chapters.summary: Final chapter, framed as the book you've just read: Elodie, the new teacher, writes down everything Dev told her, including the last line of Ruth's journal — 'Set the chair anyway.' The photographs on her wall include one more person than she remembers posing. She smiles and sets the table. Emotional beat: quiet, open-hearted ending — hospitality as the answer to horror.
